content:
In standard mathematics, a two sided ideal of a ring R is a left- and right-submodule, that is, an additive subgroupmonoid, stable under left and right multiplications by elements of R.
In mathlib, the definition of a two sided ideal in a semiring R is (essentially) RingCon R.

Although there two notions do not coincide for general semirings, they do for rings, because there is a bijection between two sided ideals and ring congruences, the ideal being the class of 0.

I wish to say that I don't find that choice absolutely reasonable; for example, it prohibits to state the last sentence.

I believe that we should have the two notions, together with the natural maps RingCon.toTwoSidedIdeal and TwoSidedIdeal.toRingCon, and their compositions under the appropriate hypotheses.
What is an additive subgroup of a semiring?
docs#TwoSidedIdeal

Yaël Dillies said:

What is an additive subgroup of a semiring?

« Les lecteurs auront corrigé d'eux-mêmes. »
The point of my rhetorical question is that two-sided ideals are misbehaved in semirings, and ring congruences are the correct generalisation
What about semigroup ideals I, such that SI <= I? Perhaps we can have an absorbing property.
the point of RingCon is that you can quotient by it, I don't see how we could get the same thing from any kind of ideal

The point of my message is that despite everything that is taught everywhere, it is a misconception to expect to quotient by a substructure. The correct principle is to quotient by an equivalence relation that is compatible with given laws. Of course, in many (really many) important cases, substructures generate natural such equivalence relations.
What is your point then? We seem to be in agreement that the substructure (TwoSidedIdeal) isn't useful and therefore we only need the equivalence relation (RingCon)?

@Antoine Chambert-Loir I also don't understand your point: the mathematically correct thing would be (as you say) to quotient wrt compatible equivalence relations, so to use RingCon. On the other hand we also want to stay close to informal math, where people mostly care about rings and use ideals because they are used to them. It seems to me that this is just un unfortunate situations where we have to choose between something non optimal for formalization (code duplication or whatever) and diverging from informal mathematical literature.
Computers ne peuvent pas se corriger eux mêmes, so we have to chose.

No, I think Antoine’s suggestion is to define docs#TwoSidedIdeal as the thing people expect, rather than an abbreviation for docs#RingCon. In other words, rather than lie to people in the definition of docs#TwoSidedIdeal, we should teach them that the right concept (if they want to cover semirings !) is docs#RingCon.
Why not get rid of TwoSidedIdeal entirely?
For the same reason we don’t want to get rid of docs#Ideal !

A similar discussion happened on a recent PR of mine, where (building on code written by Patrick at ICERM) introduced docs#LinearMap.HasFiniteRange. Oliver remarked that the better behaved notion is docs#LinearMap.HasNoetherianRange, and suggested to use this better notion but call it HasFiniteRange. While this was tempting, I ended up deciding that it was better to have both so that people can use the familiar notion but are still incentivized to use the better-behaved one.
This is also more future proof, you never know which weird use case might come up where you need the "badly-behaved" notion.
Those are very good points. The pressure in the other direction is to minimize API surface area. Because API is not super-additive in the number of concepts.
Ah, I see. This seems very reasonable (we can even generalize this to semirings, meaning an additive submnoid closed under multiplication on both sides).
We probably could keep the notation for a quotient by a two sided ideal, as an abbrev to the quotient by the corresponding RingCon.

Anatole Dedecker said:

rather than lie to people in the definition of docs#TwoSidedIdeal

What if we reframe this as "the implementation detail"? We could think of docs#TwoSidedIdeal.mk' as the definition

It is not an implementation detail, and the present docstring for docs#TwoSidedIdeal is a lie. I would prefer that people doing mathlib be conscious about what they do rather than propagating misconceptions built by the wrong extrapolation of pedagogical appropriate definitions.
Well, this is probably just an historical accident, someone forgot to fix it.

It is not an implementation detail,

What's the line you're drawing here? Are we considering it public API because of where syntax?
One easy thing we could do to help is rename mk to ofRingCon (#40776) and mk' to mk (without actually swapping out the structure field)

Eric Wieser said:

Anatole Dedecker said:

rather than lie to people in the definition of docs#TwoSidedIdeal

What if we reframe this as "the implementation detail"? We could think of docs#TwoSidedIdeal.mk' as the definition

then it comes down to "how maintainable is this implementation detail compared to the other", and i'd say the fact that docs#TwoSidedIdeal.ext is a theorem implies that

  • there is another implementation possible, more in line with the definition of Ideal.
  • that implementation is more like what "two-sided ideal" describes.

I think it is preferable to have the definition/implementation in line with the name. Since this definition does not apply to Semi(ring/whatever) anyway, i claim that there is no point mentioning RingCon.
I think this implementation is much more maintainable, because most theorems about lattices, spans, kernels, ... can be proven as a direct consequence of the ringCon versions
They are not “direct consequence”s, but rebranding of the theorems for ringCon.

Yaël Dillies said:

What is your point then? We seem to be in agreement that the substructure (TwoSidedIdeal) isn't useful and therefore we only need the equivalence relation (RingCon)?

(I wouldn't dare saying that the notion ofTwoSidedIdeal isn't useful. This would be a claim that I can't check, and maybe some colleagues can show me an interesting use of the notion of two sided ideals for semirings that I have not been able to imagine. I just wish to say that this is not the notion that gives rise to quotients. )

As a matter of fact, this discussion was prompted by a request that I make a change in #36501, from using docs#RingQuot to using either docs#TwoSidedIdeal or docs#RingCon, and the only way to be sure of what to do is to have docs#TwoSidedIdeal say what it is (and using docs#RingCon).

Ah so basically you are complaining that there are too many ways to quotient rings? Then we are rehashing the discussion that led Eric to slowly deprecate RingQuot and ultimately to suggest you do not use it in #36501 :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:
Please just use RingCon for now. This is a transitional time
#mathlib4 > Canonical way to quotient a ring ?

Antoine Chambert-Loir said:

I wouldn't dare saying that the notion ofTwoSidedIdeal isn't useful.

I guess this would be like claiming that Submonoid is not useful because you can't take quotients of it

Perhaps we should consider what our response would be to such a colleague posting "I would like to generalize TwoSidedIdeal to semirings, but the current definition produces an incorrect generalization when I do so".
@Eric Wieser I think you missed a negation in what Antoine wrote?

Did I? I meant that I think I agree that I would avoid claiming that TwoSidedIdeal.mk' would be useless in the generality of semirings, as it would be tantamount to declaring that Submonoid is useless
(with the premise that if Yael were declaring these useless, it would be because they don't give you quotients)
Ooh, nvm, I should have unified your "this" with the body of Antoine's outer negation, not the negation itself.

To the question “I would like to generalize TwoSidedIdeal to semirings, but the current definition produces an incorrect generalization when I do so”, I would first ask: what do you want to do with your generalization? If it is quotienting out, then look at docs#RingCon.Quotient.

Eric Wieser said:

Antoine Chambert-Loir said:

I wouldn't dare saying that the notion ofTwoSidedIdeal isn't useful.

I guess this would be like claiming that Submonoid is not useful because you can't take quotients of it

No that's different, because a submonoid is exactly the data of a monoid embedded in your original monoid. A two-sided ideal, however, is not the same as the data of a ring embedded into your original ring.
It's the data of a bimodule embedded into your original ring.

Yes, isn't that weird? Surely it should be defined for
an arbitrary ambient bimodule, instead of just ambient ring.
Certainly. But that's an empirical fact that Submodule R R is a very useful class of objects to consider when R is a ring.
